name: evm-dev
description: Tells whether an ERC is final or an EIP is live on Ethereum mainnet, how L2 networks, the Ethereum L1 roadmap, and consensus-only EIPs stand, writes Solidity contracts and their tests for the solc, OpenZeppelin, Foundry, and Hardhat versions a project uses, deploys them without the agent touching keys and records what was deployed, checks a release against the deployed version and the target chains, and designs contracts, wallets, multichain apps, dApp architectures, and apps built on financial standards such as ISO 20022 and FIX, from dated items checked against the official documents

interface.longDescription: Answers whether an ERC is final or an EIP is live on Ethereum mainnet, and what it lets contracts and wallets do, answers how L2 networks and rollup frameworks work and stand, what is planned for Ethereum L1, and whether consensus-only EIPs are live, writes Solidity contracts and their unit, fuzz, and invariant tests in Foundry and Hardhat projects for the solc, OpenZeppelin, Foundry, and Hardhat versions the project uses, writes deploy scripts that never touch keys and has the user sign with a hardware wallet or an encrypted keystore, records each chain's deployed addresses and checks them, compares an upgrade's storage layout and ABI with the deployed version and finds opcodes a target chain's EVM cannot run, designs smart contracts before they are written, designs wallets and signing, designs apps that run on more than one chain, plans how the parts of a dApp fit together, and designs apps built on financial standards such as ISO 20022, FIX, FpML, CDM, LEI, and XBRL. The skills work from items checked against the official documents, each with the date it was checked and its source, and re-check items that are out of date. After writing a contract, it scans the code for patterns that the project's versions changed or that no longer hold, such as tx.origin checks after EIP-7702, and builds and tests it. The test skill lists what each contract needs tested, has kiwa write the tests when it is installed, and names the functions, errors, events, access rules, and invariants no test covers; it reports a bug a test shows instead of changing the contract. The design skill asks the decisions one at a time and writes one design document that keeps the original messages and personal data off chain and puts only signed evidence on it, then checks the document's sections and reviews it against a checklist. The contract design skill writes one design document on how contracts are split, token standards, invariants, roles, upgrades, prices, transaction ordering, randomness, and external calls, from dated items on proxies, access control, price feeds, VRF, private relays, and token handling. The architecture skill writes one design document on who sends and pays for each transaction, how the app reads chain data, where data lives, the environments, the admin keys, and monitoring, from dated items on indexers, relayers, automation, testnets, multisigs, and storage, several of which have shut down. It never writes keys into files, never signs, and never changes its items.
